en.title: Library and Information Science: the whole course
en.short: What library and information science covers, how LIS degrees are organised, the main areas and how to study them.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
Library and information science (LIS) is the study of how recorded information is selected, organised, described, stored, found, used and kept. It grew from two roots. Librarianship is the work of running libraries as institutions and services. Information science studies how information behaves: how people look for it, how it is represented, and how retrieval systems work. Modern LIS also covers archives and records, digital repositories, research data and information policy.

The central idea is connection. The subject is not mainly about books as physical objects. It is about putting the right information in front of the right person at the right time, in a usable form. That is why cataloguing, classification, reference work and retrieval sit at the centre of the course.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Length, title and award differ by country and institution, so check your own department handbook and the regulator’s list.

In Nigeria, universities usually offer a four-year BSc or BLIS in a department of library and information science, often within education or social sciences. Polytechnics offer the ND and HND, usually two years each, with industrial attachment. The Librarians’ Registration Council of Nigeria (LRCN) registers practising librarians; the Nigerian Library Association (NLA) is the professional association. Postgraduate awards are the MLS or MLIS, then the PhD.

In the United Kingdom, CILIP accredits programmes. In the United States and Canada, the entry-level professional qualification is usually a master’s accredited by the American Library Association, and the bachelor’s is often in another subject. South African universities set their own combinations, and LIASA is the professional body.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The introductory stage builds vocabulary and context. It begins with what LIS is and the history of libraries and librarianship, from ancient collections to modern public and national libraries. Then come types of libraries and information centres, and information sources and formats: print, audio-visual and digital; primary, secondary and tertiary. An introduction to the organisation of knowledge explains why documents must be described and grouped. Information technology foundations, information literacy and user education, and data literacy with basic statistics give you the tools to serve users. The stage closes with the profession itself.

The core stage is the professional skill set. Descriptive cataloguing covers standards for describing items, such as AACR2, RDA, ISBD and MARC. Classification and subject access covers schemes such as the Dewey Decimal Classification, the Library of Congress Classification and Ranganathan’s Colon Classification, plus subject headings. Collection development and acquisitions, reference and user services, and information retrieval follow. Then archives and records management, preservation and conservation, digital libraries and repositories, and library management and organisation. Information law and ethics, research methods, automation and integrated systems, marketing and advocacy, and the services of academic, special, public and school libraries complete it.

At master’s level the work becomes more theoretical and research based: advanced theories of information and society, information policy and digital governance, research data management and data curation, and advanced research methods leading to a dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Practise the tools, not just the terms. Catalogue three books yourself using a current standard. Classify them and note the notation. Build a small spreadsheet or database of records. Run a search and record how many relevant items you found, so that precision and recall stop being abstract words.

Visit different kinds of library and ask staff what they actually do in a day. Read one professional journal, so you see current concerns.

Keep rules and law current. Cataloguing standards, copyright law and data protection law change, and they differ by country. Always cite the edition and the year, and check the official source before relying on a rule.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Students often think LIS is only about shelving books, or treat library science and information science as the same thing. Cataloguing and classification are also confused: cataloguing describes an item, classification places it in a scheme.

A classification scheme is a constructed system, not a natural order, and it carries the assumptions of its makers, so learn to notice bias. Do not assume that one country’s copyright or data protection law applies everywhere.

Preservation and conservation are not synonyms: preservation is the wider policy, conservation is the treatment of damaged items. Archives and libraries are different institutions with different principles. Finally, do not design a service or a system without asking the user.

keyPoints: LIS is about connecting people with the information they need, not about books as objects.
Cataloguing describes an item; classification places it in a scheme; they are different skills.
Degree length, title and accreditation differ by country, so check your own handbook and regulator.
Standards, copyright and data protection law change and differ by country, so cite the edition and year.
Practise the tools by cataloguing, classifying, searching and building records, not only by memorising definitions.
Preservation is the wider policy; conservation is the treatment of damaged items.

en.title: What Is Library and Information Science?
en.short: Data, information, knowledge and wisdom, LIS as discipline and profession, the information lifecycle and library functions.

sections.heading: Data to wisdom
sections.text: Data are raw facts or symbols without context, such as the number 31. Information is data that has been organised or interpreted, for example “the store has 31 bags of rice left”. Knowledge is understanding gained by connecting information with experience and rules: the manager knows that 31 bags will last about a week at current sales. Wisdom is the judgement to act well, such as reordering before the holiday rush. These four levels are often called the DIKW hierarchy. The borders are not fixed, and writers define them slightly differently.

sections.heading: Discipline and service
sections.text: Library and information science (LIS) is both an academic discipline and a service profession. As a discipline, it studies how information is created, selected, organised, stored, retrieved, used and preserved, and how people behave with information. As a profession, it applies that knowledge to help people find and use reliable information. LIS draws on computing, management, education and law, but it has its own questions and methods.

sections.heading: Information lifecycle
sections.text: The information lifecycle is the journey of information from creation to use and beyond. A common model runs: creation or collection; processing and organisation; storage; retrieval; use; and disposal or preservation. A library may receive a new book, catalogue it, place it on a shelf, help a reader find it, and later repair, replace or withdraw it. Digital records follow a similar path, with added questions of format and access.

sections.heading: Functions and myths
sections.text: Libraries select and acquire materials, organise them for finding, provide access and loans, answer enquiries, teach users, preserve collections, and support community needs. A common misconception is that LIS is only shelving books or that libraries are quiet storehouses. In fact the field is about connecting people with information in many formats. Another myth is that the internet makes libraries unnecessary; good search still needs selection, evaluation and organised access. LIS also deals with records, data and digital collections, not books alone.

keyPoints: Data are raw facts; information is organised data; knowledge connects information with experience; wisdom is sound judgement.
LIS is both an academic discipline and a service profession.
The information lifecycle runs from creation or collection through organisation, storage, retrieval and use to preservation or disposal.
Libraries select, organise, provide access to, and preserve information in many formats.
LIS is not only shelving books, and libraries are not made unnecessary by the internet.
Good library service connects people with reliable information and helps them use it.

en.title: History of Libraries and Librarianship
en.short: From ancient archives and Timbuktu manuscripts to print, professional associations and digital libraries.

sections.heading: Archives and manuscripts
sections.text:
Libraries grew out of archives, meaning records kept for rulers, temples and trade. Clay tablets survive from Mesopotamia, including the library of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal at Nineveh in the 7th century BCE. Papyrus rolls were collected at Alexandria in Egypt from the 3rd century BCE.

In Africa, families and mosques in Timbuktu, in present-day Mali, built manuscript collections from about the 13th century. The al-Qarawiyyin library in Fez, Morocco, is linked to a mosque and school founded in the 9th century. Every book was copied by hand, so collections were small and access was restricted.

sections.heading: Print and wider access
sections.text:
Printing with movable type appeared in China and Korea before Europe; the Jikji was printed in Korea in 1377. In Europe, Gutenberg’s press at Mainz, around 1450, made books cheaper and more plentiful.

Libraries then moved from locked cases and chained books toward wider access. England’s Public Libraries Act of 1850 allowed towns to fund free libraries, and later open shelves replaced closed ones. In Africa, colonial and missionary libraries came first, followed by national and university libraries, many of them after independence.

sections.heading: Becoming a profession
sections.text:
Librarianship became a profession through associations, training and shared standards. The American Library Association was founded in 1876 and the Library Association in Britain in 1877. IFLA, the international federation, was founded in 1927.

Nigeria’s first library school opened at the University of Ibadan in 1960, and the Nigerian Library Association was founded in 1962. Professional education, codes of ethics and common cataloguing rules turned library work into a recognised career with its own body of knowledge.

sections.heading: The digital shift
sections.text:
Computers entered libraries in the 1960s, when the MARC format made catalogue records machine-readable. Online catalogues replaced card catalogues, and the web in the 1990s brought remote access, e-journals and digital libraries.

Storage changed from tablet to scroll to codex (bound book) to printed book to digital file. Access changed from restricted to public to remote. Case: a student in Lagos can read a digitised Timbuktu manuscript, a 19th-century printed book and today’s e-journal without visiting three separate buildings.

keyPoints: Libraries began as archives and manuscript collections kept by rulers, temples and mosques.
Hand copying kept collections small and access restricted.
Print made books cheaper and helped open libraries to the public.
Professional associations and library schools, from the late 1800s onward, established librarianship as a career.
Computers and the web shifted storage from print to digital files and access from local to remote.
African library history includes Timbuktu manuscripts, al-Qarawiyyin, and post-independence national libraries.

en.title: Types of Libraries and Information Centres
en.short: Compare public, academic, school, special and national libraries, archives and information centres.

sections.heading: Main library types
sections.text: A library is an organised collection of information sources and services. A public library serves a whole community, usually free at the point of use and funded mainly by government, whether local, state or national. An academic library serves a university or college, supporting teaching and research for students and staff; it is usually funded by the institution. A school library serves pupils and teachers in a primary or secondary school and is funded by the school. A special library serves one organisation, such as a bank or hospital, is funded by it, and meets specialised needs. A national library is usually established by law to collect and preserve a country’s published heritage and to provide national records of publications. Details vary by country; check official sources.

sections.heading: Archives and centres
sections.text: An archive holds records created by an organisation or person and kept because they have continuing value. Its users are often historians, officials and researchers, and its mission is preservation and evidence, not general reading. An information centre, sometimes called a documentation centre, collects, organises and disseminates information for a defined group. It may be part of a company, ministry, NGO or research project. For example, an NGO in Nairobi might run an information centre on water and sanitation for field staff and partner communities. Its collection would stress reports and practical guides, not novels.

sections.heading: How type shapes practice
sections.text: The institution’s mission shapes collection policy. A public library buys popular fiction, children’s books and community-language material. An academic library buys textbooks, journals and databases. A special library buys narrow technical sources. Archives follow rules on origin and retention rather than buying. Staffing follows users and services: school libraries need teacher-librarian skills, special libraries need subject knowledge, archives need records expertise. Service priorities differ too: lending and reading programmes in public libraries, research support in academic libraries, alerting users to new information in information centres, and access to preserved records in archives. Budgets vary by country and year.

keyPoints: A library’s type is defined by its mission, users, funding and services.
Public libraries serve whole communities and are usually government funded.
Academic, school and special libraries usually serve their parent institution and are funded by it.
National libraries collect a country’s published heritage and provide national records of publications.
Archives preserve records of continuing value, while information centres disseminate information to a defined group.
The institution’s mission shapes collection policy, staffing and service priorities.

en.title: Information Sources and Formats
en.short: Primary, secondary and tertiary sources, print and electronic formats, evaluation criteria and reference materials.

sections.heading: Three levels of sources
sections.text: Primary sources are original, first-hand material: research articles that report a new study, interviews, letters, diaries, photographs, official records and raw data. Secondary sources interpret or analyse primary material: textbooks, review articles and biographies. Tertiary sources help you find or summarise primary and secondary work: bibliographies, indexes, abstracts, dictionaries, encyclopaedias and directories. The lines can blur. A textbook may reprint a primary document. Ask what the item itself does, not only what it is called.

sections.heading: Print and electronic
sections.text: Print sources are physical objects such as books, journals and maps. They need no device or power, and their pages stay fixed. Electronic sources are accessed through a device, often online. They can be searched, linked and updated, and reached remotely, but they depend on electricity, connectivity and licences. A library may hold the same title in both formats. Choose the format that suits the task, the reader and the available access.

sections.heading: Evaluating a source
sections.text: Evaluate authority by asking who wrote or published the item and what qualifications or review process support it. Check currency: the date of publication or update, and whether the topic needs recent information. Consider coverage: scope, depth, audience and missing aspects. Look for bias: purpose, funding, language, viewpoints and what is left out. A case: Amina, a first-year student in Kano, compares two websites on irrigation. One names an author and a university, gives a date and cites sources. The other has no author or date and sells equipment. She uses the first for background and checks its claims in a textbook.

sections.heading: Reference or circulating
sections.text: Reference materials are kept for consultation, usually inside the library, and are not normally borrowed. Examples are dictionaries, encyclopaedias, directories, atlases and indexes. Circulating materials can be borrowed, such as subject books, textbooks and novels. Policies differ, so check the catalogue record and loan rules. Reference works give quick facts and pointers; circulating works support longer study.

keyPoints: Primary sources are original material; secondary sources interpret them; tertiary sources point to or summarise them.
Print and electronic formats differ in access, searchability and dependence on power or licences.
Evaluate authority by the author, publisher and review process.
Check currency against the information need, not only the date.
Assess coverage and bias, including purpose, funding and omitted views.
Reference materials are for consultation and usually not borrowed; circulating materials can be borrowed.

en.title: Organising Knowledge: An Introduction
en.short: Classification, cataloguing, bibliographic records, call numbers and the path from catalogue to shelf.

sections.heading: Why organise a collection
sections.text:
A library collection is useful only if a reader can find a known item and discover related items. Classification groups items by subject and gives each group a notation, a short code. Cataloguing describes each item and records access points, such as author, title and subject.

Without these tools a large collection becomes a pile. The catalogue is the index to the collection, not the collection itself.

sections.heading: Records and access points
sections.text:
A bibliographic record is the catalogue entry for one item. It normally gives author, title, edition, publisher, year, ISBN, subject headings, call number and location, and the catalogue also shows the loan status. Subject headings are terms chosen from a fixed list that describe what an item is about, so subject access means searching by topic rather than by exact title.

An OPAC (online public access catalogue) is a library’s online catalogue. A record may have several access points, which are the fields a reader can search.

sections.heading: Call numbers and shelves
sections.text:
A call number is the item’s address on the shelf. It usually combines a classification number for the subject with a book number, often from the author’s name, and sometimes a year. Items are shelved in ascending call-number order: first the class number, then the book number.

Shelf labels and guiding show where each range begins and ends. Reference, reserve and oversize items may sit elsewhere.

sections.heading: From search to shelf
sections.text:
A reader searches the catalogue by author, title or subject. The record gives the call number and location. The reader notes both, goes to the named collection, follows the class number to the shelf range, then reads along the shelf in call-number order until the exact number is reached.

For example, an invented record shows call number 338.1 OKO and location Main Stacks. The reader goes to the 300s, then 338, then .1, then OKO. If the item is not there, check the record’s status and ask staff; a loan or a misshelved item may explain it.

keyPoints: Classification groups related subjects and gives each group a notation.
Cataloguing describes an item and records access points such as author, title and subject.
A bibliographic record is the catalogue entry for one item, including its call number and location.
A call number is the shelf address, usually a class number plus a book number.
Items are arranged in ascending call-number order within each collection.
Subject access lets a reader search by topic through controlled subject headings.

en.title: Information Technology Foundations
en.short: Hardware, software, networks, the internet, databases and digitisation in library work.

sections.heading: Hardware and software
sections.text:
Hardware is the physical equipment: computers, servers, scanners, printers, barcode readers and storage drives. Software is the set of instructions that tells the hardware what to do, such as the operating system, a word processor or a library management system.

In a library, hardware stores and displays information, while software organises and retrieves it. For example, a barcode reader sends a number to the library system, which records a loan. Together they support storage and service delivery.

sections.heading: Networks and internet
sections.text:
A network connects computers so they share files, printers and an internet connection. A local area network (LAN) covers one building; a wide area network (WAN) links branches. The internet is a global network of networks.

Networks support communication by email and messaging, and access to online journals and catalogues. They allow remote services, such as renewing a loan. Reliable bandwidth and security matter for library service delivery.

sections.heading: Databases
sections.text:
A database is an organised collection of data that can be searched and updated. A library catalogue is a database of records. Each record has fields, such as author, title, subject and shelf mark.

A database management system (DBMS) lets you add, edit, query and sort records. Structured data supports fast retrieval. For example, a query for the subject agriculture returns all matching records. Databases underpin catalogues and borrower records.

sections.heading: Digitisation basics
sections.text:
Digitisation converts analogue material, such as print, photographs or audio, into digital files. Steps include selecting, preparing, scanning or photographing, checking quality, describing with metadata, storing and backing up. Metadata is data about the file, such as title, date and rights.

Digitisation supports preservation of fragile originals and wider access. Worked example: a library scans 500 photographs; if each file is about 20 MB, total storage is 500 × 20 = 10,000 MB, about 10 GB. Keep a backup copy.

keyPoints: Hardware is physical equipment; software is the instructions that run it.
Networks share resources; the internet connects networks globally.
A database stores structured records that can be searched and updated.
Digitisation turns analogue items into digital files with metadata.
These tools support storage, retrieval, communication and service delivery.
Back up digital files and check quality during digitisation.

en.title: Information Literacy and User Education
en.short: Defining information literacy, search strategy, source evaluation, citation, plagiarism and user education.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text: Information literacy is the ability to recognise an information need, then find, evaluate, use and share information effectively and ethically. It is broader than computer skills: it includes critical thinking about where information comes from and what it is for. A first-year student who can plan a search, judge a source and cite it correctly is becoming information literate.

sections.heading: Search strategy
sections.text: A search strategy is a planned approach to finding information. Start by stating the question and breaking it into concepts. List keywords and synonyms. Use Boolean operators: AND narrows a search by requiring both terms, OR widens it by accepting either term, and NOT removes a term. Use quotation marks for phrases, and truncation (for example, librar* finds library, libraries and librarian) where the database allows. Choose a suitable database or catalogue, then filter by date, language or peer review. Keep a record of what you searched.

sections.heading: Evaluating and citing
sections.text: Evaluate every source for authority (who wrote it), accuracy (evidence and references), currency (date), objectivity (purpose and bias) and coverage. Peer review means experts checked a scholarly article before publication. Cite all ideas, data and words that are not your own or common knowledge. Citation styles such as APA, Harvard, MLA and Chicago differ; follow your department’s guide. Plagiarism is presenting someone else’s work, words or ideas as your own. It includes copying without acknowledgement and poor paraphrasing. Keep notes with full source details so you can cite later.

sections.heading: User education
sections.text: User education means planned activities that teach people to use library resources and become independent learners. Methods include library orientation and tours, workshops, credit-bearing courses, one-to-one consultations, online guides and point-of-need help at the desk. Good programmes are sequenced: they start with basic orientation, then teach search skills, then advanced evaluation. A concrete case: a first-year student writing about social media and students could attend a workshop, search a database with AND and OR, evaluate two sources, and cite them in APA. The librarian’s aim is not to find information for the student but to build skills the student can reuse.

keyPoints: Information literacy is the ability to recognise an information need and to find, evaluate, use and share information ethically.
A search strategy breaks a question into concepts, keywords and synonyms, then combines them with Boolean operators.
AND narrows a search, OR widens it, and NOT excludes terms.
Evaluate sources for authority, accuracy, currency, objectivity and coverage.
Cite all borrowed words and ideas in the style your department requires; plagiarism is presenting them as your own.
User education uses orientation, workshops, courses and online guides to help users become independent learners.

en.title: Data Literacy and Basic Statistics
en.short: Data types, frequencies, mean, median, mode, percentages, and reading and presenting simple library data.

sections.heading: Data and variables
sections.text: Data literacy is the ability to read, understand and present data honestly. Data are either categorical or numerical. Categorical data place items in named groups, such as student or staff, or by faculty. Numerical data are counts or measurements. Counts are discrete, such as the number of loans; measurements are continuous, such as time spent at a desk. A frequency is the number of times each value or category occurs. A percentage expresses a part of a whole: part ÷ whole × 100.

sections.heading: Descriptive statistics
sections.text: Descriptive statistics summarise a set of values. The mean is the sum divided by the number of values. The median is the middle value when the values are put in order. The mode is the most frequent value. For example, daily library visits over five days were 120, 150, 130, 160 and 140. The total is 700, so the mean is 700 ÷ 5 = 140 visits. In order, 120, 130, 140, 150, 160, the median is 140. No value repeats, so there is no mode. If 50 of 200 users joined an orientation, that is 50 ÷ 200 × 100 = 25 per cent.

sections.heading: Reading tables and charts
sections.text: When reading a table, check the title, source, units, column headings and totals. In a chart, check axis labels and scales. A bar chart compares categories; a pie chart shows parts of one whole; a line chart shows change over time. A cut or uneven axis can exaggerate small differences, so read the scale before drawing conclusions.

sections.heading: Presenting service data
sections.text: To present simple service data, use a short table with category, count and percentage. State the period and the denominator, such as September 2025, 200 registered users. Round consistently and keep the raw counts. For example, 80 of 200 users asked for help finding journals: 80 ÷ 200 × 100 = 40 per cent. Do not compare raw counts from groups of different sizes without also giving rates.

keyPoints: Data literacy means reading, understanding and presenting data honestly.
Categorical data are named groups; numerical data are counts or measurements.
Frequency is a count of occurrences; percentage = part ÷ whole × 100.
Mean = sum ÷ number of values; median = middle value in order; mode = most frequent value.
Check titles, units, labels, totals and axis scales before trusting a table or chart.
Present service data with counts, percentages, the period and the denominator.

en.title: The Library and Information Profession
en.short: Roles, career paths, associations, CPD, service values and professional conduct.

sections.heading: Roles and career paths
sections.text:
Library and information work covers roles in user services, cataloguing and metadata, collection development, systems, archives, research support, teaching and management. Career paths run through public, academic, school and special libraries, archives, digital repositories and knowledge management.

Plan by reading job descriptions, volunteering or interning, and asking practitioners. Titles and entry requirements vary by country, so check current employer and national body requirements.

sections.heading: Professional and paraprofessional
sections.text:
A professional librarian normally holds an accredited library and information science qualification and may need registration or a licence. The professional plans services, selects and organises resources, teaches users, manages budgets and staff, and makes professional judgements. A paraprofessional, such as a library assistant or technician, carries out defined tasks under supervision, for example shelving, issuing books or basic cataloguing.

The boundary differs between countries and employers. In Nigeria, the Librarians’ Registration Council of Nigeria regulates librarians; other countries have their own regulators or professional associations.

sections.heading: Associations and CPD
sections.text:
Professional associations support members, set standards, publish guidance and speak for the profession. Examples include IFLA (International Federation of Library Associations and Institutions), the Nigerian Library Association, CILIP (Chartered Institute of Library and Information Professionals) in the United Kingdom and ALA (American Library Association) in the United States.

Continuing professional development (CPD) is planned updating of knowledge and skills after qualification. It can include courses, conferences, mentoring, reading, reflective writing and a portfolio. Some associations and regulators require CPD for renewal; rules vary, so check current requirements.

sections.heading: Values and conduct
sections.text:
Service values include equitable access, confidentiality of user enquiries, intellectual freedom, accuracy, respect for privacy and commitment to users’ information needs. A code of conduct turns values into expected behaviour: act with integrity, avoid conflicts of interest, keep skills current and follow the law.

Case: Amina, a library assistant in Kano, receives a request for a reader’s borrowing history. She explains that records are confidential and refers the request to the librarian, who checks policy and law.

keyPoints: Library and information work offers roles in services, metadata, systems, archives, teaching and management.
Professional librarians usually hold an accredited LIS qualification and may need registration; paraprofessionals do defined tasks under supervision.
Professional associations set standards, publish guidance and represent members.
CPD is planned lifelong learning after qualification and may be required for renewal.
Service values include equitable access, confidentiality, intellectual freedom and respect for privacy.
A code of conduct translates values into expected behaviour and helps guide decisions.

en.title: Descriptive Cataloguing
en.short: Bibliographic description, access points, AACR2 and RDA, MARC, authority control and catalogue maintenance.

sections.heading: Description and access
sections.text: Descriptive cataloguing records an item so users can find and identify it. Bibliographic description covers title and statement of responsibility (the names of authors or editors), edition, publication details, physical description, series and standard identifiers such as ISBN (International Standard Book Number). Access points are names, titles or codes under which a record is filed or searched, for example the author’s name or title. In AACR2 (Anglo-American Cataloguing Rules, second edition) the main entry is the fullest entry, usually under the author’s name, with added entries (extra access points) for others; RDA (Resource Description and Access) prefers authorised access point and treats access points more equally.

sections.heading: AACR2 and RDA
sections.text: AACR2 was widely used in English-speaking countries from 1978. RDA, first released in 2010, replaced AACR2 in many libraries. RDA is a content standard: it says what to record, not how to display it. It covers print and digital resources. Local dates differ, and some libraries still use AACR2 or a mixture.

sections.heading: MARC and authority
sections.text: MARC, Machine-Readable Cataloguing, is a format for encoding catalogue records in a computer. MARC 21 is common; other MARC formats exist. Most data fields have a tag, indicators and subfields. Authority control keeps names and titles consistent by choosing one authorised heading, recording variant forms, and linking related headings. An item by “Chinua Achebe” may have the authorised heading “Achebe, Chinua, 1930-2013”; variant forms point to it. This gathers works by one person.

sections.heading: Maintenance and variation
sections.text: Catalogue maintenance keeps the catalogue accurate over time. It includes adding new records, updating records of copies held, correcting errors, merging duplicate records, and withdrawing items. Good maintenance also checks authority headings and links. Rules, systems and local practices vary between libraries and countries. A library may use AACR2 or RDA, MARC 21 or another encoding, and its own online public access catalogue (OPAC) display and authority practices. Check the library’s current cataloguing manual and national standards.

keyPoints: Bibliographic description records the identifying details of an item; access points are the names or titles used to find it.
AACR2 uses main and added entries; RDA uses authorised access points and is a content standard.
RDA was first released in 2010 and replaced AACR2 in many libraries, but local dates differ.
MARC encodes catalogue records for computers, with tags, indicators and subfields.
Authority control keeps headings consistent and links variant forms to one authorised form.
Catalogue maintenance includes updating, correcting, merging and withdrawing records, and local rules vary.

en.title: Classification and Subject Access
en.short: Classification, subject indexing, DDC and LCC, subject headings, thesauri and call numbers.

sections.heading: Classification and indexing
sections.text: Classification groups documents by their main subject and gives each class a notation, the symbols used on the shelf. Subject indexing describes what a document is about, usually with words or codes in a catalogue. Both are controlled: the indexer chooses from an approved list so similar items get the same label. Classification mainly arranges shelves; indexing mainly supports searching. Good indexing records aboutness, not just the title.

sections.heading: DDC and LCC
sections.text: The Dewey Decimal Classification (DDC), first published by Melvil Dewey in 1876, has ten main classes numbered 000 to 900. It is hierarchical and decimal: longer numbers mean narrower subjects. The Library of Congress Classification (LCC) uses letters and numbers, such as H for social sciences. It was developed for the Library of Congress and suits large research collections. DDC is common in public, school and many academic libraries; LCC is common in large university libraries, especially in North America. Both are revised, so editions and local practice vary.

sections.heading: Headings, thesauri, call numbers
sections.text: Subject headings are controlled terms, often pre-coordinated, meaning several concepts are combined in one string, such as "Food supply -- Nigeria". Library of Congress Subject Headings (LCSH) is a large general list; Sears List of Subject Headings is a simpler list for smaller libraries. A thesaurus is a controlled vocabulary showing broader, narrower and related terms, as MeSH does in medicine. A call number is the shelf address: class notation plus a book number, often from the author’s name. Classification supports browsing because related subjects sit together; subject headings support precise catalogue retrieval. A student wanting "food security in Nigeria" can browse the food supply class and search the heading "Food security -- Nigeria". Interdisciplinary works may need several headings or a main-class choice.

keyPoints: Classification groups by main subject and arranges shelves; subject indexing describes aboutness for catalogue search.
DDC uses ten decimal classes numbered 000 to 900; LCC uses letters and numbers.
DDC is common in public, school and many academic libraries; LCC is common in large research libraries, especially in North America.
Subject headings are controlled terms; LCSH and Sears are examples.
A thesaurus links broader, narrower and related terms.
A call number combines class notation with a book number and gives the shelf address.

en.title: Collection Development and Acquisitions
en.short: Policies, selection, acquisition workflows, licensing, budgeting, weeding and evaluation of library collections.

sections.heading: Policy and selection
sections.text:
Collection development is the planned building of a library’s collection. A collection development policy is a written statement of scope, formats, selection criteria, gifts, challenges, weeding and who decides. It makes decisions consistent.

Selection chooses items. Selectors weigh user needs, quality, currency, cost, access and preservation. They use reviews, requests, usage data and profiles. For example, a polytechnic library serving engineering and business may buy current e-books for heavy demand and fewer costly print reference sets, while keeping local history for preservation.

sections.heading: Acquisition and licensing
sections.text:
Acquisition obtains materials. A typical workflow is: receive a request, verify details, check holdings, choose a supplier, order, receive, check the item and invoice, catalogue it, then pay. Methods include firm orders, approval plans, standing orders, subscriptions, donations and exchange.

Licensing is a contract for electronic resources. Key terms include authorised users, access, interlibrary loan, perpetual access, privacy, cancellation and price increases. Licence law varies by country, so check the institution’s legal office.

sections.heading: Budget and evaluation
sections.text:
Budgeting allocates funds across formats. Allocations must not exceed the total. If a materials budget is 100,000 units, 60,000 for books, 30,000 for journals and 10,000 for preservation sums to 100,000. With 200,000 for journals and 40,000 each, five cost 200,000. A 10% rise makes each 44,000, so four cost 176,000 and five would cost 220,000.

Collection evaluation uses usage statistics, circulation, interlibrary loan and surveys. Cost per use is cost ÷ uses. A 44,000 subscription used 200 times costs 220 per use.

sections.heading: Weeding and balance
sections.text:
Weeding removes damaged, outdated, little-used, duplicated or superseded items. Criteria include condition, currency, usage, space and community needs. Do not weed unique, local or archival material without checking preservation policy.

The balance is never fixed. User needs may favour multiple copies and fast access; cost may favour shared licences; preservation may favour stable formats and controlled storage. Cooperative buying and digital repositories can widen access while sharing cost.

keyPoints: Collection development policies make selection, licensing, weeding and evaluation consistent.
Selection balances user needs, quality, cost, access and long-term preservation.
Acquisition workflow runs from request and verification through ordering, receipt, cataloguing and payment.
Licences set authorised users, access, interlibrary loan, perpetual access and price terms, and law varies by country.
Allocations must sum to no more than the budget; cost per use = cost ÷ uses.
Weeding removes damaged or superseded items but protects unique and archival material.

en.title: Reference and User Services
en.short: The reference interview, ready and research help, print and digital sources, referral and service ethics.

sections.heading: Reference work defined
sections.text: Reference and user services help people find, evaluate and use information. Reference work answers questions, teaches search skills and guides users to sources. It differs from general circulation, which handles membership, borrowing, returns, renewals and fines. A circulation desk may also answer simple location questions, such as where the toilets are, but it does not normally provide in-depth research help. The boundary varies by library, so staff should know local policy.

sections.heading: The reference interview
sections.text: The reference interview is a short, purposeful conversation to discover what the user really needs. The librarian listens, asks open questions that invite explanation, clarifies the subject, purpose, amount and deadline, then restates the need in their own words. Example: Amina asks for books on law. The librarian learns she is a first-year student preparing a ten-page assignment on land registration in Nigeria. That changes the search from general law to statutes, textbooks and official land records. The librarian confirms the plan before searching, so effort is not wasted.

sections.heading: Ready and research reference
sections.text: Ready reference means quick answers to factual questions, often from a dictionary, directory or yearbook. Research reference means a longer search that needs a strategy: choosing databases, keywords and filters, then evaluating and citing results. Print and digital sources complement each other. A printed place-name directory may be easier for local names, while a subscription database gives current journal articles. Digital sources are not automatically better; check authority, date, coverage and access limits.

sections.heading: Referral and ethics
sections.text: Referral means sending a user to another person, service or library when the question is outside your knowledge, collection or licence. Give the user the name, contact and what has already been checked, and follow up if policy allows. Service ethics require privacy and confidentiality, equal treatment, accuracy, and honesty about limits. Do not give legal, medical or financial advice; provide sources and explain that the user must consult a qualified professional. A librarian who cannot help should say so clearly and refer promptly.

keyPoints: Reference work helps users find, evaluate and use information; circulation handles membership, borrowing and returns.
The reference interview clarifies the real need through listening, open questions and restatement.
Ready reference gives quick facts; research reference needs a planned search strategy.
Print and digital sources should be judged by authority, date, coverage and access limits.
Refer users promptly when a question lies outside your knowledge, collection or licence.
Service ethics require confidentiality, equal treatment, accuracy and honesty about limits.

en.title: Information Retrieval: Searching and Evaluating
en.short: Information retrieval concepts, Boolean and phrase searching, indexing, ranking, recall, precision and search strategy.

sections.heading: Retrieval basics
sections.text: Information retrieval (IR) is the process of finding stored items, such as records, articles or web pages, that answer a user’s information need. A collection is the set of items searched; a query is the expression of the need. IR differs from data retrieval: it deals with uncertain relevance, so results are ranked rather than simply matched. A document is relevant if it helps the need, not merely if it contains the words.

sections.heading: Boolean and phrase
sections.text: Boolean searching combines terms with AND, OR and NOT. AND narrows: cats AND dogs requires both. OR broadens: cats OR dogs requires either. NOT excludes: cats NOT dogs removes records containing dogs. Parentheses set order, as in (cats OR dogs) AND diet. Phrase searching uses quotation marks to require adjacent words in order, such as "information retrieval". Truncation, for example librar*, widens a term to its variants. Check each database’s syntax, because symbols differ.

sections.heading: Indexing and ranking
sections.text: An index is a structured list of terms and the items that contain them, like the back-of-book index. Inverted indexes map each term to a posting list of document numbers. Indexing may use controlled vocabulary, where assigned subject terms are consistent, or natural language. Ranking orders results by estimated relevance. Common signals include term frequency, inverse document frequency, phrase position and links. A ranking formula is a model, not a guarantee of relevance.

sections.heading: Recall, precision, strategy
sections.text: Recall is the proportion of all relevant items that are retrieved. Precision is the proportion of retrieved items that are relevant. If a search finds 30 items, 18 relevant, and the collection holds 60 relevant items, recall = 18 ÷ 60 = 30% and precision = 18 ÷ 30 = 60%. High recall suits a literature review; high precision suits a quick answer. A search strategy plans concepts, synonyms, Boolean blocks, limits and a record of sources. Evaluate results for relevance, currency, coverage and bias, and check the database’s help pages for its syntax.

keyPoints: Information retrieval finds items that may be relevant, so results are ranked rather than simply matched.
AND narrows a search, OR broadens it, NOT excludes terms, and quotation marks require a phrase.
An index maps terms to the items containing them, and ranking estimates relevance.
Recall = relevant retrieved ÷ all relevant; precision = relevant retrieved ÷ all retrieved.
Use high recall for comprehensive reviews and high precision for quick answers.
Plan synonyms, Boolean blocks and limits, and evaluate each database’s results and coverage.

en.title: Archives and Records Management
en.short: Records lifecycle, appraisal, arrangement, finding aids, access, retention, archives versus libraries, ethics.

sections.heading: Archives and records
sections.text: Records are information created or received in the course of work and kept as evidence. Archives are records selected for permanent preservation because of enduring value. A library collects published or media items for use and lends them; an archive holds unique, often unpublished records, usually consulted on site under supervision. Archives also manage the records of their parent body.

sections.heading: Lifecycle and appraisal
sections.text: The records lifecycle runs from creation or receipt, through use and maintenance, to disposition: transfer to an archive or destruction. Appraisal decides which records have continuing value. It considers administrative, legal, fiscal and historical value. A retention schedule lists record series and how long each is kept. A Nigerian polytechnic records officer, Amina, might destroy routine stores requisitions after a short period, keep student transcripts long term, and transfer council minutes to the archive. Disposal must be documented.

sections.heading: Arrangement and description
sections.text: Arrangement is the physical and intellectual order of archives. Two principles guide it: provenance, meaning records from one creator are kept together, and original order, meaning the order used by the creator is preserved. Records are grouped into series, which are groups of related records. Description records the creator, content, dates and access conditions. Finding aids, such as inventories, registers and catalogues, help users find material.

sections.heading: Access, law and ethics
sections.text: Access is the right to consult records, often in a reading room. Retention and access rules protect privacy and confidentiality. Freedom of information laws, which differ by country, may open public records, while data protection laws restrict personal data. Archivists face ethical choices: copyright, sensitive records, provenance and repatriation. They should document decisions, apply restrictions fairly, and refuse to alter or conceal records.

keyPoints: Records are evidence of work; archives are records kept permanently for enduring value.
Archives differ from libraries because they hold unique, often unpublished records, usually consulted on site.
The records lifecycle runs from creation or receipt, through use and maintenance, to disposition.
Appraisal selects records for retention or destruction, guided by a retention schedule.
Arrangement follows provenance and original order, and finding aids help users locate material.
Access and retention must balance legal duties, privacy, confidentiality and ethical stewardship.

en.title: Preservation and Conservation
en.short: Causes of deterioration, preventive care, storage, reformatting, digital preservation and disaster planning.

sections.heading: Causes of deterioration
sections.text: Preservation is all action that prolongs collection life. Conservation is direct treatment or repair by a trained conservator. Deterioration has physical causes (careless handling, light, heat, unstable relative humidity or RH, water, fire), chemical causes (acidic paper, corrosive ink), biological causes (mould, insects, rodents), human causes (theft, poor storage) and technological causes (obsolete formats). Inherent vice means the material itself is unstable, as with cheap acidic paper. Light damage is cumulative and irreversible.

sections.heading: Preventive conservation
sections.text: Preventive conservation means indirect action to stop damage before it starts; it is usually cheaper than repair. Provide a clean, stable environment: moderate temperature and RH, good air circulation, and protection from sunlight and dust. Avoid sharp fluctuations. Use protective enclosures of suitable archival material. Practise integrated pest management (IPM): monitor, deny pests food and shelter, and use traps before chemicals. Train staff and ban food, drink and pens near collections. If a college library in Ibadan finds mould after rain, stop the leak, lower damp and isolate items for expert advice; do not wipe and reshelve them.

sections.heading: Storage and handling
sections.text: Store items on strong shelving away from walls, pipes and sunlight, with air space. Do not overcrowd. Keep books upright and supported; store large or fragile volumes flat. Use clean hands and follow local glove policy. Never use ordinary adhesive tape for repairs. Reformatting copies content to microfilm or digital images to reduce handling; it does not preserve the artefact. Keep a master copy, check quality and record metadata.

sections.heading: Digital preservation and disasters
sections.text: Digital preservation is active management, not one scan. Keep several copies in different places, test backups, check fixity (that files have not changed), and migrate before formats become obsolete. Record technical metadata. Disaster planning is part of risk management: identify hazards, estimate likelihood and impact, reduce risks, and write a plan with contacts, salvage priorities, supplies and training. Run drills. Recovery starts with safety, then stabilises the environment and freezes wet paper if expert help is delayed.

keyPoints: Preservation covers all actions that prolong collection life; conservation is direct treatment by a trained conservator.
Deterioration comes from physical, chemical, biological, human and technological causes, and light damage is irreversible.
Preventive conservation uses a stable environment, good housekeeping, protective enclosures and integrated pest management.
Correct storage and handling reduce wear; reformatting improves access but does not preserve the original artefact.
Digital preservation needs multiple copies, fixity checks, metadata and migration before formats become obsolete.
Disaster planning is part of risk management: identify hazards, reduce risks, plan salvage, train staff and run drills.

en.title: Digital Libraries and Repositories
en.short: Digitisation workflows, metadata, repositories, open access, access control and sustainability.

sections.heading: Digital library or website
sections.text: A digital library is an organised collection of digital objects, with selected materials, metadata, search services, and a policy for keeping the collection usable. An institutional repository is a managed store for one institution’s outputs, such as theses, articles and reports; it accepts deposits and aims to preserve them. An ordinary website publishes pages for information or promotion, but need not select, describe or preserve its contents as a collection. The boundaries are not fixed: a repository can be part of a digital library.

sections.heading: Digitisation workflow
sections.text: Digitisation turns physical or analogue items into digital files. A typical workflow is: select items and check copyright; prepare and scan or photograph them; check image quality; run optical character recognition (OCR) to make text searchable; create metadata; store master files and access copies; publish; and plan preservation. Suppose a college digitises past examination papers. It checks rights, scans, checks missing pages, records course, year and date in metadata, and keeps a master copy separate from the web copy.

sections.heading: Metadata and access
sections.text: Metadata is structured information about a resource. Descriptive metadata supports finding, for example title, creator and subject. Structural metadata shows how parts fit together, such as pages in a book. Administrative metadata covers rights, technical details and preservation. Dublin Core is a common simple element set. Repositories often let other services collect, or harvest, their metadata through a standard protocol called OAI-PMH (Open Archives Initiative Protocol for Metadata Harvesting). Access control decides who may see or download what. It uses authentication (proving identity), authorisation (granting rights), licences and embargoes, which delay release for a set period. Open access means free online access to research, but not always free to publish; authors may pay a fee, and rights still apply.

sections.heading: Open access and sustainability
sections.text: Open access is often provided by repositories (green route) or journals (gold route). Sustainability means the service can continue: stable funding, trained staff, clear policies, and digital preservation through backup, format migration and checks. Without these, links break and files become unreadable. A repository should state what it collects, who may deposit, how material is reviewed, and how it is preserved.

keyPoints: Digital libraries select, describe and preserve digital collections and offer services; repositories store one institution’s outputs; ordinary websites need not do these things.
Digitisation runs from selection and rights checking through scanning, OCR, metadata, storage, access and preservation.
Descriptive metadata supports finding, structural metadata shows how parts fit, and administrative metadata covers rights and preservation.
Access control uses authentication, authorisation, licences and embargoes.
Open access means free online access to research, not necessarily free publication.
Sustainability needs stable funding, trained staff, clear policies and digital preservation such as backup and format migration.

en.title: Library Management and Organisation
en.short: Planning, organising, staffing, budgeting, evaluation, change and governance in libraries.

sections.heading: Planning and governance
sections.text:
Management sets goals and uses people, money and other resources to reach them. Planning turns the library’s mission into objectives, actions and timetables. A strategic plan covers several years; an operational plan covers one year or less. Managers set priorities by weighing legal duties, user needs, cost, risk and expected benefit. A priority matrix scores proposals on impact and effort, ranking high impact, low effort first.

Governance is who has authority. Models include a board or trustees, a local authority, a parent institution, and a statutory national library. Decision-making models differ: the rational model compares options; incrementalism makes small changes from the current position; mixed scanning combines both. Participatory decisions involve staff; top-down decisions are faster but may miss local knowledge.

sections.heading: Organising and staffing
sections.text: Organising groups work into departments, teams and clear reporting lines. A structure may be functional, by subject, or by user group. Staffing covers job analysis, recruitment, induction, training and appraisal. A job description states duties; a person specification states required knowledge and skills. Managers delegate authority with responsibility and protect staff from overload.

sections.heading: Budgeting example
sections.text: A budget is a financial plan. Line-item budgets list expenses by type; programme budgets by activity; zero-based budgets require every cost to be justified each year. Suppose a college library has 1,200,000 units for the year. It allocates 50% to staff = 600,000; 30% to collections = 360,000; 15% to systems = 180,000; 5% to user services = 60,000. The total is 1,200,000. If a new database costs 90,000, the manager must cut elsewhere or seek extra funds; the choice should follow priorities, not habit.

sections.heading: Evaluation and change
sections.text: Evaluation compares results with objectives. Inputs are resources, outputs are services, and outcomes are changes for users. Key performance indicators (KPIs) are measures such as visits, loans or satisfaction. Change management guides people through new systems or services. Lewin’s model describes unfreezing, changing and refreezing. Communicate the reason, involve staff, train them, and review effects. Resistance is information, not disloyalty.

keyPoints: Management turns mission into plans and uses resources to meet objectives.
Governance defines who has authority; models include boards, local authorities, parent institutions and statutory national libraries.
Rational, incremental and mixed-scanning models describe different ways of deciding.
Organising sets reporting lines; staffing covers recruitment, induction, training and appraisal.
In a budget, total spending equals the sum of allocations, and each allocation should follow priorities.
Evaluation compares inputs, outputs and outcomes using key performance indicators, and change needs communication and staff involvement.

en.title: Information Law and Ethics
en.short: This summary covers copyright, privacy, access, intellectual freedom and professional ethics.

sections.heading: Copyright basics
sections.text: Copyright protects original expression, such as text, images, sound and software, once fixed in a tangible form. It gives the creator exclusive rights to copy, publish, adapt and communicate the work. Countries allow limited exceptions for teaching, research or library copying, but the rules differ. Fair use and fair dealing are names for such exceptions: limited use of a copyrighted work without the owner’s permission. The United States uses fair use; the United Kingdom and many Commonwealth countries use fair dealing. The term of protection varies, often life plus 50 or 70 years. Check your national statute and library exceptions.

sections.heading: Privacy and access
sections.text: Privacy means protecting personal data, including borrowing records and search histories. Data protection law, where it exists, requires lawful collection, a stated purpose, security, and rights to access and correction. Library codes usually treat user records as confidential. A court order or specific legal duty may require disclosure, so follow written policy and seek legal advice. Freedom of access means people can use collections and services without unnecessary barriers. It does not remove lawful limits, such as preservation, licensing or child protection.

sections.heading: Intellectual freedom
sections.text: Intellectual freedom is the right to seek, receive and share information and ideas without unjustified interference. It supports diverse collections and the user’s right to read. Libraries often handle complaints through a reconsideration policy: a written request, a staff review, and a recorded decision. Censorship is the removal or blocking of material because of its content. A small case: Ms Nakato, a librarian in Kampala, receives a complaint from Dr Okello about a health book; she keeps it on the shelf while the review committee examines it under policy. Names and facts are invented.

sections.heading: Professional ethics
sections.text: Professional ethics are standards of conduct. Codes from bodies such as IFLA and national library associations call for service, confidentiality, intellectual freedom, equal access, honesty and avoidance of conflicts of interest. Ethics is not the same as law: a legal act can be unethical, and ethical duties can be limited by law. Statutes, regulations and codes change, so check the current official text in your country.

keyPoints: Copyright protects original expression and gives limited exclusive rights, with exceptions that vary by country.
Fair use and fair dealing are different national approaches, not universal rules.
Privacy and data protection require libraries to keep user records confidential and secure, subject to lawful disclosure.
Freedom of access and intellectual freedom oppose unnecessary barriers and censorship while allowing lawful limits.
Ethics codes guide conduct but do not replace the law, and legal compliance alone may not be ethical.
Statutes, regulations and professional codes change, so check the current official source in your country.

en.title: Research Methods in Library and Information Science
en.short: Research design, qualitative and quantitative methods, sampling, data collection, analysis, ethics and reporting.

sections.heading: Designing a study
sections.text: A research design is the plan linking a question to evidence. Quantitative research measures variables and tests relationships with numbers. Qualitative research explores meanings, experiences and practices, often in words. Mixed methods combine both. In libraries, a question such as “How do students use the reference desk?” can be studied by counts, interviews, or both. The design must fit the question, time and ethics approval.

sections.heading: Methods and sampling
sections.text: The population is everyone you want to describe; the sample is the part you study. Probability sampling, such as simple random sampling, gives every member a known chance of selection and supports generalisation. Non-probability sampling, such as purposive or convenience sampling, is common in qualitative work but limits generalisation. Tools include questionnaires, interviews, focus groups, observation and document analysis. Pilot the tool, check wording, and record response rates. If 120 questionnaires are sent and 90 return, the response rate is 90 ÷ 120 = 75%.

sections.heading: Data and analysis
sections.text: Quantitative data are analysed with descriptive statistics: frequencies, percentages and means. Inferential statistics can then test relationships. Percentage = part ÷ total × 100. Mean = sum of values ÷ number of values. Qualitative data are often coded, then grouped into themes. Coding means labelling segments of text; thematic analysis means building patterns from those labels. Keep raw data and analysis notes. Do not claim more than the data show. A small survey cannot prove causation.

sections.heading: Ethics and reporting
sections.text: Research ethics protect people and trust. Seek informed consent, explain purpose and voluntariness, protect confidentiality and anonymity, avoid harm, and get institutional approval where required. Data protection rules differ by country, so check the current law and your institution’s policy. Report writing includes title, abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion, conclusion and references. Report limitations honestly. In a small case, a librarian in Ghana interviews ten students about a new reading room; she reports themes, not percentages, and removes names.

keyPoints: A research design links a clear question to evidence and must fit time and ethics approval.
Quantitative methods measure variables with numbers; qualitative methods explore meanings and experiences; mixed methods combine both.
Probability sampling supports generalisation; non-probability sampling is common but limits it.
Pilot data collection tools and report response rate as returned ÷ sent × 100.
Percentage = part ÷ total × 100; mean = sum of values ÷ number of values.
Seek informed consent, protect confidentiality, check data protection law, and report limitations honestly.

en.title: Library Automation and Integrated Systems
en.short: How integrated library systems work, their core modules, selection, migration and staff training.

sections.heading: What an ILS is
sections.text: An integrated library system (ILS), also called a library management system, is software that runs core library operations from one shared database. Catalogue records, borrower records and transactions are stored once and used by every module, which keeps data consistent. The online public access catalogue (OPAC) is the public search interface: users search by author, title or keyword, see availability, and may place holds or renew loans.

sections.heading: Core modules
sections.text: The circulation module handles borrowing: check-out, check-in, renewals, holds, due dates, fines and borrower records. It enforces loan rules such as how many items a student may borrow. The acquisitions module supports ordering, receiving, invoicing and budget tracking, and links orders to vendor records and the catalogue. The serials module manages journals and other continuing resources: subscriptions, issue check-in, claims for missing issues and prediction of the next issue. Small libraries may combine these tasks; large ones separate them.

sections.heading: Selection and migration
sections.text: System selection starts with a needs analysis: library size, workflows, budget, connectivity, language and reporting needs. Compare vendors on function, cost of licence or subscription, hosting, support and interoperability with standards such as MARC for bibliographic data. Vendors, systems and local requirements differ, so ask for demonstrations and speak to reference sites. Migration means moving data from the old system. Extract records, clean them, map fields to the new structure, test with a sample, then run in parallel before go-live. Keep a backup and a rollback plan.

sections.heading: Training and go-live
sections.text: Staff training should be role-based and practical: circulation staff practise loans and returns, acquisitions staff practise orders, and administrators learn permissions and reports. Use written procedures, short sessions and refresher training after go-live. In an invented case, a college library in Ibadan moves from a paper register to an ILS. The librarian lists must-have functions, trains two staff as champions, tests 200 sample records, corrects a date-field mapping error, and only then stops the paper register.

keyPoints: An ILS runs cataloguing, circulation, acquisitions, serials and the OPAC from one shared database.
The OPAC is the public search interface; circulation handles loans, holds and fines.
Acquisitions covers ordering and budgets; serials covers subscriptions and issue check-in.
Selection begins with a needs analysis and comparison of vendors, costs and support.
Migration requires cleaning, mapping and testing data before go-live.
Role-based training and a rollback plan reduce risk.

en.title: Information Marketing and Advocacy
en.short: User research, segmentation, promotion, advocacy, outreach and showing library value to stakeholders.

sections.heading: Research and segments
sections.text: Information marketing is the planned process of understanding user needs and designing, communicating and delivering services that meet them. It is not only advertising. It applies the marketing mix: product, price, place and promotion. User research gathers evidence through surveys, interviews, focus groups, usage data and observation. Segmentation divides a community into groups with shared needs, such as students, researchers, older people or small businesses. A segment must be large enough to serve and distinct enough to need a different message. Choose segments by need, behaviour, location or language, not by assumptions.

sections.heading: Promotion and outreach
sections.text: Promotion uses a mix of channels: notice boards, social media, email, local radio, partnerships and face-to-face events. The message should state a clear benefit and be truthful. Outreach takes services to people who may not visit, through mobile libraries, school visits, community meetings or online tutorials. A simple case: Ama, a librarian in Kumasi, Ghana, surveys senior high school students and finds that closing time and travel discourage use. She promotes a Saturday homework club through schools and WhatsApp, and reports attendance and student feedback to her funder.

sections.heading: Advocacy and value
sections.text: Advocacy means speaking publicly for the library, its users and its principles, especially to decision-makers who control budgets or policy. It builds relationships over time, not only during a funding crisis. Demonstrate value with evidence: visits, loans, database sessions, programme attendance, survey results and stories of changed outcomes. Link evidence to the funder’s goals, such as literacy, research or employment. Avoid inflated claims; state what the data show and what they do not show.

sections.heading: Stakeholder relations
sections.text: Stakeholders include users, staff, funders, governing bodies, partner organisations and the wider community. Build relationships through regular updates, open days, consultation and shared projects. Invite stakeholders to see services in use, ask for their views and report back on results. Ethical marketing protects user privacy, obtains consent for messages and refuses manipulative targeting. A library that listens, reports honestly and keeps its promises earns trust and support.

keyPoints: Information marketing matches library services to user needs and communicates their value.
User research and segmentation help libraries design relevant services and messages.
Promotion uses several channels, while outreach takes services to non-users.
Advocacy speaks for the library and its users to decision-makers and funders.
Demonstrate value with honest evidence linked to stakeholder goals, not inflated claims.
Build long-term relationships through consultation, updates and ethical handling of user data.

en.title: Academic and Special Library Services
en.short: Services in academic and special libraries, and how they differ from public libraries.

sections.heading: Two settings
sections.text:
An academic library serves a university, college or other higher education institution. Its main users are students, lecturers and researchers. A special library serves one parent organisation, such as a company, government department, research institute, hospital, law firm or museum, and its users are mainly that organisation’s staff. Both support study and investigation, but their missions and users differ.

Academic libraries sit within a university or college and support teaching, learning and research. Special libraries exist to meet the information needs of the organisation that funds them.

sections.heading: Core services
sections.text:
Collection support means making sure the right materials are available: reading lists, course reserves, e-journals, databases, subject guides and liaison with departments. Research support helps researchers find literature, manage references, plan searches and use specialist sources. User training includes orientation, workshops and short sessions on databases, the catalogue and citation tools. The mix depends on the institution.

A subject or liaison librarian is a common role: a librarian assigned to a faculty or department who understands its information needs and communicates with its staff and students.

sections.heading: Scholarly communication
sections.text:
Scholarly communication is the system by which research is created, evaluated, published, shared and preserved. Academic and special libraries support it through advice on open access, the free online sharing of research, deposit in repositories (digital archives of research outputs), copyright and publishing options, and responsible use of bibliometrics, which are measures of research output and impact.

Policies differ by country and institution. A library should point authors to its repository rules and the publisher’s terms rather than give blanket legal advice.

sections.heading: Differences from public
sections.text:
Public libraries are usually funded by government and serve everyone in a community, with general collections and community services. Academic and special libraries have a defined primary clientele, collections shaped by the parent body, and access often restricted to members.

For example, a hospital library in Ghana may hold clinical guidelines and run literature searches for doctors; a public library in the same city lends novels and children’s books to all residents.

keyPoints: Academic libraries serve universities and colleges; special libraries serve one parent organisation, such as a company, hospital or research institute.
Collection support covers reading lists, reserves, e-resources, subject guides and liaison.
Research support includes literature searching, reference management and specialist sources.
Scholarly communication covers open access, repositories, copyright and bibliometrics.
User training introduces users to databases, catalogues and citation tools.
Unlike public libraries, academic and special libraries have defined clienteles and specialised collections, often with restricted access.

en.title: Public Library and Community Services
en.short: Public library mission, needs assessment, adult and family services, outreach, digital inclusion and funding.

sections.heading: Mission and needs
sections.text:
A public library is usually a local service funded from public money and open to all. Its mission is to give free access to information, support lifelong learning, culture and social inclusion. International guidance, such as the IFLA/UNESCO Public Library Manifesto, calls it a local gateway to knowledge.

A community needs assessment is a planned way to learn what local people need. It uses surveys, interviews, focus groups, local statistics and service records. The results set priorities and reveal gaps.

sections.heading: Adult and family services
sections.text:
Adult services include literacy, job-search help, language classes, reading groups and health information. Family services support parents and children through story times, early literacy activities and homework help.

Outreach means services outside the building: mobile libraries, home delivery, pop-up points and events in markets or community centres. It reaches people who cannot visit or feel unwelcome.

For example, a library in Nakuru, Kenya, could survey residents, find that many adults want evening digital-skills classes, then change opening hours and work with a college.

sections.heading: Digital inclusion and partnerships
sections.text:
Digital inclusion means helping everyone use digital technology. It covers public computers, Wi-Fi, device lending, accessible design and digital literacy training, including help with online government services.

Partnerships are agreements with organisations, such as schools, NGOs, health services, local government, businesses and community groups. Partners share resources, skills and reach. They can extend hours or reach underserved areas. Partnerships need clear rules on privacy, data protection and commercial influence, so free access is not undermined.

sections.heading: Funding and access
sections.text:
Public library funding differs by country and locality. Sources include municipal taxes, national grants, donations, fees or a mix. Guidance generally treats core services as free, but fee rules vary.

Access barriers include distance, opening hours, charges, poor transport, disability, language, low literacy, weak connectivity and censorship. Budget cuts can reduce staff, collections and outreach. Check national and local policy, as rules and funding change.

keyPoints: A public library is a local, usually publicly funded service that supports free access to information, lifelong learning, culture and social inclusion.
A community needs assessment uses surveys, interviews, local statistics and service data to set priorities and reveal gaps.
Adult and family services include literacy, job-search help, language classes, story times and homework support.
Outreach takes services outside the building through mobile libraries, home delivery, pop-up points and community events.
Digital inclusion and partnerships extend reach through shared resources, digital literacy training and clear rules on privacy and commercial influence.
Funding and fee rules vary by country and locality, so access barriers and current policy should be checked.

en.title: School Library and Children’s Services
en.short: School library programmes, age-appropriate collections, reading promotion, information skills and teacher collaboration.

sections.heading: Programme and role
sections.text:
A school library programme is the planned services, resources and teaching a school library offers. It supports the curriculum and helps pupils learn to find, judge and use information. The library is a learning space, not only a store, where reading and inquiry are taught. Its role depends on the school’s mission, staffing and budget. Rules vary by country; check local guidelines.
