Case: Mrs Adeyemi, a librarian in Ibadan, Nigeria, plans a term programme with English and science teachers: a reading hour, a website-evaluation lesson and a water project collection.

sections.heading: Collections by age
sections.text: Children’s and young adult collections are chosen for pupils’ age, reading level and interests. Children’s books serve younger readers; young adult (YA) books serve teenagers, though age bands vary. Selectors consider language, format, cultural relevance, curriculum links and pupil requests. They apply the school’s selection policy and avoid unsuitable material. A balanced collection includes fiction, non-fiction, reference, magazines and digital resources. In multilingual settings, local-language books matter. Replace worn items and remove outdated material by policy.

sections.heading: Reading promotion
sections.text: Reading promotion means planned activities that encourage voluntary reading. Examples include book talks, displays, reading challenges, author visits, story hours and peer recommendations. The aim is to build motivation and habit, not only to test comprehension. Let pupils choose, and include popular series, graphic novels and magazines where policy allows. A reading challenge in which pupils record finished books and discuss one with a friend can work without prizes. Track participation, not book counts.

sections.heading: Teaching and collaboration
sections.text: Information skills teaching helps pupils define a question, search, evaluate sources, take notes, cite and present findings. Teach these skills within the curriculum, not as isolated library lessons. Collaboration with teachers works best when librarian and teacher plan together: shared goals, timetable, resources and assessment. The librarian may co-teach, prepare a pathfinder (a guide to sources) and help assess. Age-appropriate services match the task: picture books and guided reading for young children; databases, citation and critical evaluation for older pupils.

keyPoints: A school library programme links resources, teaching and reading to the curriculum.
Children’s and young adult collections must suit age, reading level, culture and school policy.
Reading promotion builds voluntary reading habit through choice and planned activities.
Information skills are best taught within subject lessons, not as isolated library lessons.
Librarian and teacher collaboration improves planning, teaching and assessment.
Rules, staffing and standards for school libraries vary by country, so check current guidelines.

en.title: Advanced Theories of Information and Society
en.short: Theories of information, the information society, knowledge production and critical LIS perspectives.

sections.heading: Information and society
sections.text: In information theory, following Shannon and Weaver, information is a measurable signal that reduces uncertainty; meaning lies outside the model. Social theories treat information as meaningful, situated and produced in relationships. The term information society describes societies where information work, digital networks and knowledge-intensive services become central. Daniel Bell’s post-industrial society and Manuel Castells’s network society are influential accounts. Critics say such labels can hide inequality: not everyone has the same access, skills or power to shape information.

sections.heading: Knowledge production
sections.text: Knowledge production means how new knowledge is made, validated and used. Mode 1 is discipline-based, academic and peer-reviewed. Mode 2, as described by Gibbons and colleagues, is transdisciplinary, application-driven and socially distributed. Social epistemology, associated with Jesse Shera and Margaret Egan in LIS, asks how communities and institutions shape what counts as knowledge. A university, a library and a community group may all produce knowledge, but they do not carry equal authority.

sections.heading: Critical LIS and access
sections.text: Critical library and information science draws on critical theory to ask who benefits from information systems and who is excluded. It treats access as more than a connection: access includes skills, language, affordability, privacy and the power to publish. Technology is not neutral; design choices, algorithms and licences shape visibility. Information institutions, such as libraries, archives and platforms, can widen access or reproduce inequality. An invented case: a county library in Kenya offers free internet. A trader checks market prices, but the library also logs searches and sets opening hours that exclude night workers. A critical analysis asks whose needs are served and who decides.

sections.heading: Comparing perspectives
sections.text: Functionalist views stress efficiency and social benefit. Interpretive views study meaning and everyday practice. Critical views stress power, class, gender and colonial legacies. No single theory explains all cases; use them as lenses. Ask what each theory reveals and what it hides.

keyPoints: Information theory treats information as a signal that reduces uncertainty, not as meaning.
The information society thesis says information work and networks become central, but critics stress unequal access.
Mode 1 knowledge is disciplinary; Mode 2 is transdisciplinary and socially distributed.
Social epistemology asks how institutions shape what counts as knowledge.
Critical LIS examines power, exclusion and the non-neutrality of technology.
Compare functionalist, interpretive and critical perspectives rather than treating one as complete.

en.title: Information Policy and Digital Governance
en.short: National and international information policy, data protection, copyright, open access, inclusion and governance.

sections.heading: Policy layers
sections.text: Information policy is the laws, standards, budgets and practices that shape how information is created, accessed, used and preserved. Digital governance is accountable decision-making and oversight of digital systems and data. Policy operates at institutional, national, regional and international levels. International and regional instruments, such as the Berne Convention on copyright or the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) in the European Union, set baselines or influence practice beyond their borders. Treaties like Berne bind only their member states and take effect through national law; the GDPR applies directly in EU states and can also reach some organisations outside the EU. Analyse who makes each rule, whose interests it serves, how it is enforced and what capacity exists for implementation.

sections.heading: Data and copyright
sections.text: Data protection law controls processing of personal data: collection, storage, use, sharing and deletion. Copyright gives creators exclusive rights over works, subject to exceptions such as quotation, education or preservation, which differ by country. A library cannot assume a European exception applies in Nigeria, Kenya or South Africa. Check the current national statute and any regional regime. In a case, a university library in Ghana plans to publish theses online. It must obtain permissions or use an agreed licence, remove sensitive personal data, and record decisions. Copying a European open-access policy is not enough; Ghana’s copyright and data-protection rules govern the project.

sections.heading: Open access and inclusion
sections.text: Open access means free online access to research, usually with rights to reuse, as in the Budapest Open Access Initiative. Funder and institutional mandates vary, so check the specific policy. Digital inclusion means fair access to connectivity, devices, skills and accessible content. It is a governance issue, not only a technical one: licensing, language, disability access and rural broadband affect who can use information. A policy that ignores these barriers can widen inequality even when legally sound.

sections.heading: Governance in practice
sections.text: Good digital governance uses transparency, stakeholder consultation, records of decisions, review dates and clear accountability. Ask how a policy is monitored, who can challenge it, and how complaints and breaches are handled. International frameworks bind only the states that accept them, so they are not universal law. Name the jurisdiction and check the current official source before applying a rule.

keyPoints: Information policy covers laws, standards, budgets and practices across institutional to international levels.
Digital governance requires transparency, accountability and review, not only technical systems.
Data protection law governs personal data processing and differs by jurisdiction.
Copyright gives creators rights, but exceptions such as education and preservation vary by country.
Open access and digital inclusion depend on licences, connectivity, skills, language and accessibility.
Analyse who sets a rule, whose interests it serves, how it is enforced and whether implementation capacity exists.

en.title: Research Data Management and Data Curation
en.short: Lifecycle, data management plans, metadata, repositories, open data, preservation and ethics.

sections.heading: Lifecycle and planning
sections.text:
Research data management (RDM) keeps data usable and trustworthy across the lifecycle: planning, collection, processing, analysis, sharing and preservation. Data curation is the active work of selecting, describing, cleaning and maintaining data for reuse.

A data management plan (DMP) is a written plan, often required by funders, stating data types and formats, storage and backup, access controls, retention and sharing. Update it as the project changes.

Case: Amina leads a Kenyan public health study on clinic waiting times. Her DMP names anonymised spreadsheets, encrypted storage, restricted access during the study, and deposit in the university repository after publication.

sections.heading: Metadata and repositories
sections.text:
Metadata is structured information about data: title, creator, date, method, variables, licence and access conditions. It makes data findable and reusable. The FAIR principles (findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable) set out how data should be prepared for reuse. Common standards include Dublin Core, DataCite and DDI.

A data repository stores data and metadata, assigns a persistent identifier such as a DOI, and controls access. Repositories may be institutional, subject-specific or general. Libraries often run institutional repositories and advise on metadata, formats and deposit.

sections.heading: Open data and preservation
sections.text:
Open data is data shared for reuse under clear legal terms, often a Creative Commons licence such as CC BY, or the CC0 public domain dedication. Personal, commercial or security-sensitive data may need controlled access or may not be shared.

Digital preservation keeps data usable over time through format migration, checksums to detect corruption, redundant copies and documentation. The OAIS reference model describes these functions. Libraries curate by setting file-naming rules, recording versions and reviewing retention.

sections.heading: Ethics, law and libraries
sections.text:
Ethical constraints include informed consent, privacy, anonymisation and avoiding harm. Legal constraints vary by country: data protection law, copyright and database rights, and funder rules. For example, Nigeria’s Data Protection Act 2023 and the EU General Data Protection Regulation set duties for personal data.

The library’s role is practical: training, DMP review, metadata advice, repository management, preservation and licence help. Librarians do not replace ethics committees or legal advisers, but connect researchers to them.

keyPoints: RDM covers planning, collecting, processing, sharing and preserving data across the lifecycle.
A data management plan states formats, storage, access, retention and sharing before research begins.
Metadata makes data findable and reusable; standards include Dublin Core, DataCite and DDI.
Repositories assign persistent identifiers and manage access; libraries often run or advise on them.
Open data needs lawful permission and a clear licence; sensitive data may need controlled access.
Libraries support researchers through DMP advice, metadata, curation, preservation and ethics guidance.

en.title: Advanced Research Methods and Dissertation
en.short: Advanced qualitative, quantitative and mixed methods, sampling, ethics and dissertation defence.

sections.heading: Planning the study
sections.text: A master’s dissertation in library and information science starts with a proposal: a short document that states the problem, question, aims, methods, timetable and ethics. An advanced design matches the question to the method. Qualitative research explores meaning and context, often through interviews or focus groups. Quantitative research measures variables and tests hypotheses with numbers. Mixed methods combines both, often using triangulation to compare or expand findings. Triangulation means checking findings from more than one source or method. State the paradigm, the underlying worldview, and justify the mix.

sections.heading: Sampling and instruments
sections.text: Sampling is choosing participants from a population. Probability sampling, such as simple random or stratified sampling, supports statistical generalisation. Non-probability sampling, such as purposive or snowball sampling, suits qualitative work but limits generalisation. Instrument design means writing questionnaires or interview guides. Check validity, whether an instrument measures what it claims, and reliability, whether it gives consistent results. Pilot the instrument. For a proportion, a common sample size formula is n = z² p(1−p) / e². With 95% confidence (z = 1.96), p = 0.5 and e = 0.05, n = 3.8416 × 0.25 ÷ 0.0025 = 384.16, so 385 before finite population correction, which reduces n when the population is small.

sections.heading: Analysis and ethics
sections.text: Qualitative analysis often uses thematic analysis: coding transcripts, grouping codes into themes and checking negative cases, meaning cases that do not fit the themes. Quantitative analysis uses descriptive statistics and inferential tests, such as chi-square or regression, chosen to fit the data. Mixed analysis integrates the strands in a joint display, a table that sets the qualitative and quantitative results side by side. Ethics require informed consent, voluntary participation, confidentiality, secure data storage and ethics committee approval. Data protection law differs by country, so check the current rule. Report limitations honestly.

sections.heading: Writing and defending
sections.text: The dissertation usually has chapters: introduction, literature review, methodology, results, discussion, conclusion and references. Follow your department’s format. A viva voce is an oral defence before examiners. Prepare a short summary, know your methods and limitations, and answer questions calmly. Present tables and figures clearly. Keep a record of corrections.

keyPoints: A proposal for an original study states the problem, question, aims, methods, timetable and ethics.
Match the design to the question: qualitative for meaning, quantitative for measurement, mixed methods for both.
Probability sampling supports generalisation; non-probability sampling limits it.
Check validity, reliability and pilot your instrument.
For a proportion, n = z² p(1−p) / e²; with z = 1.96, p = 0.5 and e = 0.05, n = 385 before finite population correction.
Ethics approval, informed consent, confidentiality and honest reporting are required; the viva voce is an oral defence.
